p.seg: Heaven produced the people and instituted their measures.
It measured great and small to establish rectitude,
weighed light and heavy to reach the utmost,
clarified root and branch to establish the mean,
established the mean to compensate for loss,
compensated for loss to know contentment,
□ ranks to clarify grades and extremes,
extremes to rectify the people,
rectified inner and outer to complete the mandate,
rectified high and low to conform to governance.
Governance by internal □,
□□ from near,
flourishing from far.
Far and near are completely exhausted at the end.
□ subtle compensation is in □□,
the division of the subtle is in clarity.
The enlightened king therefore reveres the subtle and conforms to the division.
Dividing in order to know harmony,
knowing harmony to know joy,
knowing joy to know sorrow.
Sorrow and joy to know wisdom,
inner and outer to know people.
All people are born with likes and dislikes.
If they get a little of what they like, they are pleased;
if they get much of what they like, they are joyful.
If they encounter a little of what they dislike, they are worried;
if they encounter much of what they dislike, they are sorrowful.
What all people like and dislike:
living things are liked,
dead things are disliked.
When people's likes reach a point where they do not yield,
and they do not follow what they like,
they will certainly violate laws and be unable to serve their superiors.
When people's dislikes reach a point where they do not yield,
and they do not discard what they dislike,
they will certainly violate laws and be unable to serve their superiors.
If this is universally practiced,
there will still be unruly people.
How much more so if it is said that by being able to get rid of their dislikes and obtain what they like,
can the people be at peace?
If they do not □ strength,
how can they seek it?
If they compete with strength, it will be a government of strength;
a government of strength means no yielding;
no yielding means no rites.
Without rites,
even if they get what they like,
will the people be joyful?
If they are not joyful,
then it is what they dislike.
If people cannot tolerate likes and dislikes,
they cannot make divisions in order;
if there is no order, there is usurpation;
if there is usurpation, there is war.
If there is war, how can the old and young be nourished?
How can pain, sickness, death, and bereavement be relieved?
How can they mutually assist each other?
The enlightened king therefore sets grades to the utmost to decide likes and dislikes,
teaches the people to divide in order,
promotes and raises those who excel in strength,
employs the strong and nourishes the old.
The young and old have their rewards,
thus the people mutually assist each other.
Indeed, excelling in strength cannot succeed without the multitude;
the multitude cannot be a multitude without harmony;
harmony cannot be established without the mean;
the mean cannot be careful without rites;
rites cannot be practiced without music.
The enlightened king therefore has no joy that is not for people,
no sorrow that is not for people,
thus the people are numerous.
When people are numerous,
many rewards and few punishments
is the beauty of governance.
Many punishments and few rewards
is the evil of governance.
Many punishments lead to distress;
few rewards lead to scarcity.
Scarcity and distress make for no ugliness,
and thus teaching does not arrive.
Therefore, the people's lord clarifies ugliness to lengthen the lineage of descendants.
Descendants follow customs,
birds and beasts become benevolent,
the land is suitable and the timing is right for heaven,
the myriad things proceed in order.
The beginning of order is the beginning of prosperity.
When order transforms, it is compliant.
Therefore, there is no compliance that is not strict.
When the old and young are completed, the righteousness that arises is called ultimate compliance.
Heaven gave birth to the people and established the great mandate.
The mandate oversees virtue,
rectifying it with fortune and misfortune.
It establishes an enlightened king to bring them into accord,
saying:
The great mandate has constancy,
and the small mandate is daily perfected.
When perfected, one is reverent;
when constant, one is expansive.
Being expansive and revering the mandate,
then the measure reaches its extreme.
Indeed, if one oversees virtue and righteousness and is bestowed with blessings and emoluments,
and blessings and emoluments are human matters,
how can one not be warned?
If one is warned and repents of past wrongs,
then the measure reaches its extreme.
Indeed, if one oversees unrighteousness and is afflicted with misfortune,
which is a human matter,
how can one not be warned?
If one is warned and repents of past wrongs,
then the measure reaches its extreme.
Indeed, when people are born and are ugly and not enlightened,
and there is nothing to enlighten them,
how can they not be ugly?
If one has ugliness but strives to avoid ugliness,
then the measure reaches its extreme.
Indeed, when people are born and love life,
and there is nothing to nourish them,
how can they not be exhorted?
If they are exhorted with loyalty,
then the measure reaches its extreme.
Indeed, when people are born and hate death,
and there is nothing to awe them,
how can they not be afraid?
If they are afraid and accept instruction,
then the measure reaches its extreme.
When the six extremes are connected,
the six gaps are all blocked.
Connecting the Dao and connecting with Heaven to rectify people,
there is nothing better for rectifying people than having an extreme.
There is nothing better for connecting with Heaven than being without an extreme.
If connecting with Heaven has an extreme, it will not be majestic.
If it is not majestic, it will not be manifest.
If rectifying people has no extreme, they will not be trusted.
If they are not trusted, they will not act.
An enlightened king manifests Heaven and trusts people to measure achievements,
and uses the land to benefit them.
If he makes trusted people fear Heaven,
then the measure reaches its extreme.
Indeed, the Dao of Heaven is threefold,
and the Dao of man is threefold.
Heaven has mandate, misfortune, and fortune.
Man has ugliness, mourning attire (fúmǐn), and axes.
Using human ugliness to correspond to the mandate of Heaven,
using fúmǐn to correspond to the fortune of Heaven,
and using axes to correspond to the misfortune of Heaven –
these six directions and three narratives,
their extreme is one.
If one does not know this, one cannot exist.
If the mandate is pushed to its extreme, the people will fall.
If the people fall, they will neglect the mandate.
If they neglect the mandate to admonish their superiors,
then it will be close to chaos.
If fortune is pushed to its extreme, the people will be greedy for emoluments.
If the people are greedy for emoluments, they will seek good.
If they seek good, they will not act.
If misfortune is pushed to its extreme, the people will become like ghosts.
If the people are like ghosts, there will be excessive sacrifices.
If there are excessive sacrifices, families will be ruined.
If ugliness is pushed to its extreme, the people will rebel.
If the people rebel, they will harm others.
If they harm others, it is unrighteous.
If rewards are pushed to their extreme, the people will exploit their superiors.
If they exploit their superiors, the people will have no deference.
If they have no deference, they will not be compliant.
If punishments are pushed to their extreme, the people will be full of deceit.
If they are full of deceit, they will not be loyal.
If they are not loyal, there will be no recompense.
All these six [situations]
are dangers to governance.
Therefore, an enlightened king manifests the mandate to command them, saying:
The great mandate punishes generations;
the small mandate punishes the self.
No blessing is greater than acting righteously.
No misfortune is greater than excessive sacrifices.
No ugliness is greater than harming others.
No reward is greater than trusting righteousness.
No deference is greater than exploiting superiors.
No punishment is greater than greed and deceit.
The enlightened kings of antiquity
upheld these six [principles]
to shepherd the myriad people.
The people used them without error.
They soothed them with benevolence,
harmonized them with impartiality,
gathered them with compassion,
entertained them with music,
cautioned them with rites,
taught them with arts,
awoke them with governance,
moved them with affairs,
exhorted them with rewards,
awed them with punishments,
governed them with loyalty,
and acted through expediency.
If expediency is not lawful,
loyalty is not loyal,
punishments are not obeyed,
rewards do not follow labor,
affairs do not inspire awe,
governance is not achieved,
arts are not excessive,
rites have their proper times,
music is not full,
sorrow does not reach its extreme,
impartiality is not uniform,
and benevolence does not tolerate harm to people.
All these are of the type that disrupt things.
If benevolence tolerates harm to people,
people cannot overcome harm.
Harm is worse than death.
If impartiality is uniform, it is not harmonious.
If sorrow reaches its extreme, it leads to destitution.
If music is full, it leads to wantonness.
If rites have no proper times, they are not valued.
If arts are excessive, they harm talent.
If governance is achieved, it does not last long.
If affairs inspire awe, they yield few merits.
If rewards follow labor,
but labor is not sufficient;
if rewards follow the law and are appropriate,
rewards are not necessarily appropriate.
If actions follow the law through expediency,
actions are not necessarily done by understanding expediency.
Expediency is used to know the subtle.
The subtle is used to know the beginning.
The beginning is used to know the end.
Heaven has its constant nature,
people have their constant compliance.
Compliance lies in what can be changed,
nature lies in what cannot be altered.
What cannot be altered can be based upon,
that basis lies in likes and dislikes.
Likes and dislikes give rise to changes,
changes in customs give rise to constants.
Constants then give rise to ugliness,
ugly fate gives rise to virtue.
The enlightened king thereupon established governance to rectify them.
People are born with customs and constants,
they take customs as constants,
and constants as caution.
If people are born in the middle,
they take accustomed constants as constant.
Indeed, for people, custom is constant,
it begins from blood and qi.
The enlightened king, from the customs of blood, qi, eyes, and ears, clarifies ugliness.
When ugliness is clarified, people delight in righteousness,
delighting in righteousness leads to the supreme.
Honoring the worthy without exhaustion,
sorrow and joy are not excessive.
The people know its ultimate extent,
and it extends to their descendants.
The people then have antiquity.
The ancients relied on the people to comply with them.
People gather in groups without selection,
governance begins with this.
It begins with antiquity,
and ends with antiquity.
Following the ancients and aspiring to the present,
is the ultimate of governance.
Governance emphasizes the present,
laws emphasize the ancient.
Obstinacy and greed lead to doubt,
doubtful intentions lead to dichotomy.
Balancing dichotomy leads to triangulation,
triangulation and quantification lead to discretion.
Discretion in numbers leads to multitude,
multitude of difficulties leads to sincerity.
Sincere virtue leads to caution,
caution in the subtle leads to beginning with respect and ending with reverence,
then one will not be distressed.
Distress lies in obtuseness,
temptation lies in the king.
The people then become heedless,
heedlessness then leads to lack of clarity.
Sorrow and joy are not timely,
the four indications are not manifest,
the six extremes are not subdued,
the eight policies are not compliant,
the nine virtues have treachery,
the nine treacheries are not moved,
all things do not arrive.
Indeed, rites are not upheld without overcoming,
not completed without joy.
The people are thus born lacking.
□ Likes and dislikes have four indications:
joy, delight, sorrow, grief.
Actuate them according to rules,
express them with culture,
accomplish them with names,
implement them with transformation.
Six extremes:
fate, listening, fortune, reward, calamity, punishment.
If the six extremes are not excessive,
the eight policies will be harmonious.
Eight policies:
husband, wife, father, son, elder brother, younger brother, lord, minister.
If the eight policies are not contrary,
the nine virtues will be pure and respectful.
Nine virtues:
loyalty, trustworthiness, reverence, firmness, gentleness, harmony, steadfastness, integrity, compliance.
Compliant words are called governance,
compliant governance is called success,
successful deceit is called treachery.
Monitoring things is with the eyes,
monitoring sounds is with the ears.
Both ears and eyes can be doubted,
doubtful words have a pivot,
the movement of the pivot has harmony,
harmonious intentions are unequal,
the myriad people have no law.
□□ lies in pardon,
□ restoration lies in antiquity.
In antiquity, enlightened kings upheld the law to clarify the obscure,
obscure kings upheld obscurity to abolish the law.
The upholding of principles is one,
but the achievements and merits are different.
Therefore, the enlightened king reveres the subtle and complies with distinctions.
People are born with desires and dislikes,
with joy and sorrow,
with virtues and rules.
Rules have nine gatherings,
virtues have five treasures.
Sorrow has four endurance,
joy has three abundance.
Dislikes have two faults,
desires have one extreme.
The extreme has seven matters,
the fault has three suppressions,
the abundance has three frequencies,
the endurance has four teachings,
the treasure has five greatnesses,
the gathering has nine considerations.
Nine considerations:
First, take and allow people to move.
Second, honor heroes to observe.
Third, invigorate the sluggish to assist the people.
Fourth, loan officials for attachment.
Fifth, people say ritual is necessary.
Sixth, comings and goings take this.
Seventh, merchants trade capital.
Eighth, farmers gain good profit.
Ninth, □ favor can be swayed.
Five greatnesses:
First, great knowledge leads strategies.
Second, great martial prowess and courage.
Third, great craftsmen perform tasks.
Fourth, great merchants offer bribes.
Fifth, great farmers provide loans.
Four teachings:
First, guard with trust.
Second, rely on kin by age.
Third, take relatives and release from fetters.
Fourth, delight in life and restore the body.
Three frequencies:
First, frequent salaries are substantial.
Second, hidden blessings reach the spiritual extreme.
Third, retain the self and disperse the genuine.
Three suppressions:
First, eliminate military faults and ugliness.
Second, confirm kin and investigate estrangement.
Third, borrow time for crucial matters.
Seven matters:
First, leap over faults and trust will.
Second, assist and extract from defiled schemes.
Third, gather doubts and obstruct affairs.
Fourth, elevate subordinates to awe the multitude.
Fifth, dwell in generosity and humble oneself.
Sixth, overcome blockages and prepare for victory.
Seventh, record soldiers and avoid war.
One extreme is only for the flourishing Way of affairs,
opening stores and launching expeditions.
Expeditions have three solemnities and seven trusts,
one leader and two governors,
three securities and twelve arrivals.
Three solemnities:
First, cut off spiritual connections and break cities.
Second, divine oddities for prosperous action.
Third, turtle shell divination follows ominous omens.
Seven trusts:
First, the caution of benevolence in dispersal.
Second, the complete ingenuity of wisdom.
Third, the refined wealth of courage.
Fourth, the sparse bribes of clans.
Fifth, the shallow capital of merchants.
Sixth, the small accumulation of farmers.
Seventh, the struggle for favor among the nobility.
One leader:
Overcoming the beginning of power.
Two governors:
First, planting kindness without resentment.
Second, employing this concern.
Three securities:
First, settled residence and safe treasury.
Second, nobles contribute and receive cloth.
Third, punishing crimes and distributing wealth.
Twelve arrivals:
First, bows and second, arrows return to archery.
Third, wheels and fourth, chariots return to driving.
Fifth, salted fish and sixth, fresh fish return to storage.
Seventh, pottery and eighth, metallurgy return to the stove.
Ninth, tree trunks and tenth, craftsmen return to the forest.
Eleventh, bamboo and twelfth, reeds return to their season.
Three solemnities and seven trusts,
one leader and two governors,
three securities and twelve arrivals.
The Way of expedition is fully laid out,
nothing is not falling.
Falling things are taken as a match,
only then is there eternal inquiry.
How urgent, how urgent!
Later, opportunities are lost.
In a year of abundance and ample grain,
guest sacrifices are grand;
grand bells are silenced;
fine clothes are discouraged;
domestic animals are restrained;
surplus sons are assigned to crafts;
palaces and city walls are repaired and made ready;
choice vegetables are provided;
thus the year is complete.
In a lean year with insufficient grain,
guest sacrifices are moderately grand;
only bells and drums are played, not fine music;
the three pastures and five treasuries are used to supplement;
all luxuries are suspended;
surplus sons are assigned to farming;
thus order is maintained.
In a year of famine,
then one works diligently without entertaining guests;
sacrifices are meager;
there are no bells or drums for music;
all luxuries are forbidden;
carriages are not assembled early;
chariots are not intricately carved;
military preparations are not restricted;
people's profits are not excessive;
taxes are levied on merchants and travelers
to relieve the poor;
inquiries are made according to the locality;
cooked food is not sold;
aid is distributed to assist those in need, to pacify the destitute;
thus distress is relieved.
In a great famine,
there are prayers but no sacrifices;
the state does not proclaim music;
hope does not fill the ravines;
punishments are not carried out;
dwellings are used to relieve the poor;
the ruler personally inspects the regions;
ministers discuss grain purchases;
surplus sons manage transportation;
□ are opened for communal eating;
the people do not hoard grain, which is called having relief.
The people are made to raise only cattle and sheep;
among the people there is great sickness and confusion;
killing [is prohibited];
no one is pardoned;
men guard the borders;
military prohibitions are not issued;
the five treasuries do not provide meals;
funeral rites are without measure;
sacrifices are with meager provisions;
rites are without music;
palaces are not curtained;
marriages are not made at the proper time;
guest travelers are given positions and gifts.
A great state does not lose its majesty;
a small state does not lose its humility;
an enemy state does not lose its power;
to attack the barbarians in dangerous places,
to annex small states and suppress disorder,
to □ the strong and attack the weak and strike the unjust,
these are the principles of military action (Wǔ).
To attack the disorderly, to attack the sick, to attack the epidemic,
these are the proper applications of Wǔ.
To assist the worthy,
to seize the rebellious,
to encourage those who act,
to thwart the lazy,
to intimidate the fearful,
to urge on the ambitious,
these are the uses of Wǔ.
Handsome men destroy the elders,
beautiful women destroy the empress,
lustful images destroy □,
excessive crafts destroy the times,
excessive music destroys correctness,
excessive words destroy righteousness,
these are the destructions of Wǔ.
To pardon their multitudes,
to achieve their retribution,
to comfort their □,
to assist their coffers,
these are the tactics of Wǔ.
To bait the enemy with divisions,
and to illuminate their stores,
to attack and assist virtue,
to pursue the power of the times,
these are the esteems of Wǔ.
To disrupt their farming in spring,
to attack their harvest in autumn,
to seize their wheat in summer,
to chill their clothes in winter,
to desire ease in spring and autumn,
to desire speed in winter and summer,
these are the timings of Wǔ.
The long triumphs over the short,
the light triumphs over the heavy,
the straight triumphs over the crooked,
the many triumph over the few,
the strong triumphs over the weak,
the full triumphs over the hungry,
the solemn triumphs over the angry,
the first triumphs over the last,
the swift triumphs over the slow,
these are the triumphs of Wǔ.
To pursue the barbarians without restraint,
not to engage a cornered foe,
when strength is exhausted and morale is depleted,
then it is easy to conquer,
this is the pursuit of Wǔ.
Having conquered others,
to raise flags and announce,
to command officials to prohibit looting,
not to dare to invade or oppress,
titles and ranks are not diminished,
fields and dwellings are not reduced,
each settles their own relatives,
the people submit as if transformed,
this is the pacification of Wǔ.
When the hundred surnames all submit,
to lay down arms and promote virtue,
to flatten their treacherous obstacles,
to destroy their submission,
the four quarters fear and submit,
possessing the entire realm,
this is the stabilization of Wǔ.
To contemplate tranquility, to act and triumph,
truly culture is the guideline.
To make a clear proclamation throughout the land,
wherever the banner is,
to collect weapons and release bribes,
not to move their villages,
officials and schools subordinate to their duties,
relying on their hundred officials,
public goods, whether few or many,
to provide relief and gifts to poor scholars,
to rescue the emaciated and treat the sick,
to evenly distribute taxes and apportion fields,
to command men to resume their duties,
thereby abandoning worries and shame.
Orphans and widows without recourse
receive ample provisions and all rejoice.
All inquire about distant relatives,
recording their whereabouts.
To select those of the same clan name,
to position them as heads of the lineage,
leading with the fifteen,
to pacify with □ peace,
to educate with clear trust,
as if gaining parents,
to govern with leniency;
who would say they do not listen?
Listening to words without regret,
following and nurturing in obscurity,
obscurity and clarity then converse,
at this time, truly Wǔ.
The dead think of returning to life,
the living think of returning to their place,
people know they are not abandoned,
love and guard their proper households,
upper and lower harmonious and cooperative,
no enemy not subdued,
holding that jade *guī*,
to dwell in its space.
The common people all cultivate,
children and adults without assistance,
not obstructing their gains,
connecting their territories,
the people's longing for soldiers
is like waiting for parents.
Therefore, the world is stabilized in one day,
possessing the four seas.
There are seven methods of warfare:
first, governing; second, attacking; third, invading; fourth, campaigning; fifth, arraying; sixth, battling; seventh, fighting.
One skilled in governing does not attack.
One skilled in attacking does not invade.
One skilled in invading does not campaign.
One skilled in campaigning does not array.
One skilled in arraying does not battle.
One skilled in battling does not fight.
One skilled in fighting is not defeated.
Governing has nine grounds.
Grounds have four kin and five harmonies.
Attacking has nine openings.
Openings have four misfortunes and five advantages.
Invading has seven considerations.
Considerations have four gatherings and three retrenchments.
Campaigning has seven opportunities.
Opportunities have four seasons and three inspirations.
Arraying has seven approaches.
Approaches have three sorrows and four pardons.
Battling has eleven invigorations.
Invigorations have six hardships and five safeguards.
Fighting has eleven guests.
Guests have six expansions and five contingencies.
The four kin:
first, inner relatives;
second, outer relatives through marriage;
third, friends;
fourth, allies.
The five harmonies:
first, there is Heaven with no evil;
second, there are people with no gaps;
third, those with common good solidify their bonds;
fourth, those with common hatred assist each other;
fifth, distant dwellings are not slighted.
All these nine
are the grounds for governing.
The four misfortunes:
first, attacking at an improper heavenly time;
second, attacking unsuitable terrain;
third, attacking virtuous people;
fourth, attacking when weapons are disadvantageous.
The five advantages:
first, gaining benevolence;
second, gaining wisdom;
third, gaining courage;
fourth, gaining talent;
fifth, gaining skill.
All these nine
are the openings for attacking.
The four gatherings:
first, considering them with benevolence;
second, conciliating them with joy;
third, gathering feudal lords from all sides;
fourth, setting up sieges with trust.
The three retrenchments:
first, comparing men and women;
second, ordering artisans;
third, respecting the dead.
All these seven
are the considerations for invading.
The four seasons:
first, spring, disrupting their farming;
second, summer, consuming their grains;
third, autumn, taking their harvests;
fourth, winter, freezing their stores.
The three inspirations:
first, governing for harmonious times;
second, campaigning against chaos for order;
third, campaigning against hunger for satiety.
All these seven
are the opportunities for campaigning.
The three sorrows:
first, demanding without gain;
second, losing the populace;
third, shunning one's own kin.
The four pardons:
first, conquering people must bring gain;
second, obtaining awe and regaining trust;
third, people delight in preserving their lives;
fourth, pardoning what the people detest.
All these seven
are the approaches for arraying.
The six hardships:
first, benevolence is invigorated through action;
second, wisdom is invigorated through the Way;
third, martial prowess is invigorated through courage;
fourth, the army is invigorated through its soldiers;
fifth, the commander of the ranks invigorates the charioteers;
sixth, the archery master invigorates the ranks.
The five safeguards:
first, clarifying benevolence to embrace forgiveness;
second, clarifying wisdom to assist strategy;
third, clarifying martial prowess to employ courage;
fourth, clarifying talent to command soldiers;
fifth, clarifying skill to manage officials.
All these eleven
are the invigorations for battling.
The six expansions:
first, clear commands;
second, clear disgrace;
third, clear rewards;
fourth, clear punishments;
fifth, advantageous weapons;
sixth, striving for completion.
The five contingencies:
first, drumming to create doubt;
second, preparing for what comes;
third, auxiliary chariots raising flags;
fourth, gathering the advice of the foresters;
fifth, moving last to manipulate them.
All these eleven
are the guests for fighting.
Without striving, there is only harm;
with merit, there is no defeat.
Awe-inspiring and grand martial power.
It says:
Across the four directions,
awe-inspiring might brings tranquility.
Heaven creates martial power,
to cultivate military weapons,
to assist righteousness and rectify opposition, following the celestial order.
The five officials oversee their governance,
to prevent any losses.
City walls and moats,
their height and thickness are measured.
Once treading on enemy ground,
be thoroughly cautious of their calamities.
Respect their stern ruler,
then battle and pardon.
The ten arts must be clear,
add to them the ten grounds,
and no enemy will be undefeated.
Arrays like clouds spread,
invasions like wind moving.
Light chariots guard the flanks,
on the two sides of the battle.
When our army is in distress,
no one is not resolute.
The ten arts:
first, great support;
second, clear obedience;
third, surplus children;
fourth, long-term prosperity;
fifth, attacking people;
sixth, residual punishments;
seventh, three doubts;
eighth, secret letters;
ninth, using the few;
tenth, stirring up grievances.
The ten grounds:
first, cultivating benevolence;
second, overcoming desires;
third, entertaining guests;
fourth, connecting travelers;
fifth, kin and relatives;
sixth, the helpless;
seventh, colleagues;
eighth, assessing skill;
ninth, □ ability;
tenth, beneficial affairs.
Arts and grounds are used for campaigning,
this is called strong assistance.
Responding to Heaven and following the times,
times have cold and heat.
Wind, rain, hunger, and illness,
people then cannot settle.
Scattering and dispersing without defeat,
farmers become merchants.
Entrusting them with excessive pleasures,
bribing them with beautiful women.
If the ruler is weak,
□ to the city walls.
High earthworks overlooking the interior,
day and night unceasing.
Square formations combining efforts,
how can they resist?
Though easy, one must be respectful,
this is called clear martial power.
High city walls are difficult to level,
fill them with earth.
Open a path for passage,

In the second month of the King's first year of reign,
the King was at Fēng.
He secretly ordered a messenger to inquire of Zhōu Gōng Dàn, saying:
"Alas!
Day and night I maintain Shāng,
but secretly, not openly.
Who will bring harmony?
It is like the autumn of the year;
now I do not gather its harvest.
What is to be done?"
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"This lies in virtue,
and reverence lies in Zhōu.
It is the Mandate of Heaven;
may the King revere the Mandate.
Estranged kin,
no ten harmonies,
no repeated failures.
It is to maintain bright virtue without negligence;
negligence cannot be reversed.
Your cultured father was diligent and respectful.
With trepidation, how can one be reverent?
What to like, what to dislike?
At this time, irreverence is perilous!"
The King bowed and said:
"Indeed!
I have heard that the state has four estrangements, five harmonies, seven failures, nine dependencies, and ten excesses.
It is not that without reverence, one does not know them.
Now, these words are truly corrective.
I will not discard good to block myself,
but will strictly adhere to these clear warnings."
The Duke of Zhōu bowed and said:
"This is to follow Heaven.
Heaven sent awakening to Chéng;
Chéng sent dependencies to Shāng;
Shāng now produces Gé;
Gé has Zhōu on its right.
May the King clearly use words that open harmony;
who would dare not correct their words?
The four estrangements are:
first, internal and external collusion;
second, foreign marriages;
third, officials and teachers colluding;
fourth, sharing sorrow but not labor.
The five harmonies are:
first, having Heaven as the state's foundation;
second, having Earth as righteousness;
third, sharing likes as joy;
fourth, sharing dislikes as sorrow;
fifth, distant regions not contending.
The seven failures are:
first, establishment in abolition;
second, abolition in reverence;
third, comparison at the gate;
fourth, flattery within;
fifth, selfishness without;
sixth, selfishness in public matters;
seventh, public good not being upheld.
The nine dependencies are:
first, spirits that do not accept offerings;
second, virtue that has something to guard;
third, talents that are not appointed to office;
fourth, affairs that are not balanced;
fifth, two parties that must contend;
sixth, wealth that has distinctions;
seventh, greed that has limits;
eighth, preferences that are fulfilled;
ninth, enemies that are victorious.
The ten excesses are:
first, excessive governance ruins the state;
actions are not timely,
and the people are not protected.
Second, excessive preferences ruin righteousness;
words do not align,
and the people are not in harmony.
Third, excessive music ruins virtue;
virtue is not pure,
and the people lose their constancy.
Fourth, excessive movements ruin propriety;
propriety is insufficient,
and the people do not yield.
Fifth, excessive intermediaries ruin ritual;
rituals are not uniform,
and the people do not align.
Sixth, excessive colors ruin clothing;
clothing is not regulated,
and the people are not compliant.
Seventh, excessive literature ruins the classics;
the classics do not serve as models for teaching,
and the people are not categorized.
Eighth, excessive power ruins precedents;
precedents do not regulate officials,
and the people have no laws.
Ninth, excessive lending ruins duties;
the hundred officials' orders are not heeded.
Tenth, excessive craftiness ruins utility;
utility is insufficient,
and all intentions are not achieved.
Alas!
If the ten excesses are not averted,
it is perilous!
Shāng is now in this state;
it is indeed in this order.
If the Mandate is not heeded, it is perilous!
It is like a person who issues orders;
to revoke an order without pardon
is to revoke the Mandate of Heaven,
to terminate the achievements of your cultured father,
and to tolerate the suffering of the people.
This is inauspicious.
It is like a farmer tending his field;
if he focuses on plowing but not weeding,
weeds will occupy it.
When autumn comes and he harvests nothing,
birds will feast on it.
If people then go hungry,
who will pity them?"
The King bowed and said:
"Your words are corrective!
Alas!
Day and night, trembling with fear,
what is there to fear that is not the Way?
What is there to dislike that is not right?
Irreverence is perilous!"
On the day of the waxing crescent moon in the first month of the King's second year of reign,
the King summoned Zhōu Gōng Dàn and said:
"Alas!
Day and night I am concerned for Shāng,
not knowing the ultimate principles of the Way.
I reverently listen to diligently manage all under Heaven."
The Duke of Zhōu bowed, prostrated himself, and said:
"My cultured father
followed and illuminated the Three Ultimates,
personally observed the Four Scrutinies,
followed and applied the Five Phases,
warned and viewed the Seven Compliances,
and complied with the Nine Records of the Way.
When the Three Ultimates are clear,
the Five Phases are constant.
When the Four Scrutinies are right,
the Seven Compliances are discerned.
When the forces of the Heavenly Way are clear,
the Nine Records are all appropriate.
If one plans with compliant virtue,
nothing will fail to be carried out.
The Three Ultimates are:
first, Heaven with its nine stars;
second, Earth with its nine regions;
third, Man with his four sides.
The Four Scrutinies are:
first, the eye scrutinizes the ultimate;
second, the ear scrutinizes sounds;
third, the mouth scrutinizes words;
fourth, the heart scrutinizes thoughts.
The Five Phases are:
first, black positioned as water;
second, red positioned as fire;
third, cyan positioned as wood;
fourth, white positioned as metal;
fifth, yellow positioned as earth.
The Seven Compliances are:
first, compliance with Heaven gains timely opportunities;
second, compliance with Earth gains assistance;
third, compliance with the people gains harmony;
fourth, compliance with benefit makes wealth sufficient;
fifth, compliance gains clear assistance;
sixth, compliance with benevolence prevents failures;
seventh, compliance with the Way yields achievements.
The Nine Records are:
first, the constellations record the days;
second, the lunar lodges record the months;
third, the sun records virtue;
fourth, the moon records punishments;
fifth, spring records birth;
sixth, summer records growth;
seventh, autumn records killing;
eighth, winter records storage;
ninth, the year records the end.
Timeliness can be observed from Heaven,
and by not missing the opportune moment, one knows good and ill fortune."
The King bowed and said:
"Indeed!
I have heard that in the ancient teachings and classics, there are rules,
but without the right time, there are no corrective words.
My daily correction is insufficient."
In the third year of Wáng's reign,
on the *bǐngchén* day of the second month, which was the new moon,
the Wáng was in Hào.
He summoned Zhōu Gōng Dàn and said:
“Alas!
Be respectful!
I have heard it said:
‘What cultivation is not personal?’
The person has Four Positions and Nine Virtues.
‘What selection is not of men?’
Men have Ten Evils.
‘What is there without counsel?’
Counsel has Ten Dissipations,
will they not hinder us?
‘What caution is not in speech?’
Speech has Three Trusts.
Trust gives rise to treasures,
treasures make things precious,
and things, when complete, become vessels.
Beautiful precious things are not constant;
that which is valued,
trust in it without fail.
Act with spirit,
embellish with treasures,
comply with affairs,
enlighten the multitude with preparation,
and rectify flaws to employ them,
so that all may avoid suffering.
The Four Positions are:
First, steadfastness (*dìng*);
second, uprightness (*zhèng*);
third, tranquility (*jìng*);
fourth, reverence (*jìng*).
Reverence in position is grand!
Tranquility prevents errors,
uprightness in position is not abandoned,
steadfastness secures a peaceful dwelling.
The Nine Virtues are:
First, filial piety (*xiào*);
let sons be reverent,
then their counsel will not be disordered.
Second, fraternal respect (*tì*);
fraternal respect knows order,
order creates proper relationships,
proper relationships do not soar too high,
and the high will not collapse.
Third, compassion and benevolence (*cíhuì*);
this understands elders and youths,
understanding elders and youths,
one delights in supporting the old.
Fourth, loyalty and forbearance (*zhōngshù*);
these are called the Four Decorum.
Words spread widely and profoundly,
intentions are firm and unyielding.
Fifth, impartiality and uprightness (*zhōngzhèng*);
these are called discretion and decisiveness,
knowing how to choose to supplement deficiencies.
Sixth, respect and humility (*gōngxùn*);
these are called tolerant virtues,
adapting to circumstances with law,
securing the superior without malice.
Seventh, broad-mindedness and generosity (*kuānhóng*);
these are called a spacious mind,
measuring virtue with righteousness,
delighting in abundant blessings.
Eighth, gentleness and integrity (*wēnzhí*);
these are called enlightened virtues,
joy and anger without deficiency,
the master will then submit.
Ninth, martial readiness (*jiānwǔ*);
these are called clear punishments,
benevolent yet able to endure,
honoring the great principles of Heaven.
When the Nine Virtues are widely prepared,
future generations will have renown.
The Ten Evils are:
First, extreme poverty hindering tranquility;
second, drunkenness hindering governance;
third, eloquent benevolence hindering wisdom;
fourth, shifting purity hindering clarity;
fifth, death-defying courage hindering martial prowess;
sixth, expansive sincerity hindering trust;
seventh, vying for praise hindering modesty;
eighth, flattering the multitude hindering reputation;
ninth, obstinate foolishness hindering resolution;
tenth, stubborn isolation hindering integrity.
The Ten Dissipations are:
First, abandoning [...] actions then leak;
Third, shallowness and deceit leading to schemes being discovered;
fourth, careless speech and light intentions,
then harming plans and establishments;
fifth, acting forgivingly but not desiring,
not worrying about one's plans;
sixth, extreme speech without measure,
then one's plans are wasted;
seventh, treating relatives as strangers,
then one's plans are futile;
eighth, wandering thoughts and considerations,
all affairs then go astray;
ninth, being foolish and self-confident,
not knowing what to uphold;
tenth, not letting go of great agreements,
forgetting relatives for profit.
The Three Trusts are:
First, spring giving birth and summer growing without partiality,
the people then are not bewildered.
Second, autumn withering and winter killing with regularity,
governance then flourishes.
Third, man governs all things,
the virtues of things are their virtues,
this is called the ultimate trust.
As for the rest,
when trust has reached its extreme,
desires still exist,
existing without knowing righteousness.
When desires exist for beauty and possess righteousness,
this is called giving rise to treasures.”
Zhōu Gōng bowed, kowtowed, and rose, saying:
“I am capable of producing treasures,
but I fear that without them,
my descendants will fail.
If I can produce treasures
but cannot produce benevolence,
I fear I will have no successors to cherish.
If the Wáng produces treasures
but I fear losing the Wáng's assembly,
the Way will then be abandoned.”
The Wáng bowed and said:
“When one speaks,
I encourage them to secure their position,
and broaden their teachings.
If treasures are used to cause disorder,
it is not my fault.
If the superior establishes honor and emoluments,
he does not worry about a lack of benevolence.
Benevolence to cherish emoluments
is truly a canonical principle.
Having obtained their emoluments,
their reputation also increases.
When superiors and subordinates all strive,
who will not compete in benevolence?
As for the counsel for descendants,
let treasures be the constant.”
In the third year of Wáng's reign,
the Wáng was in Fēng.
Counsel and words were reported and heard.
The Wáng summoned Zhōu Gōng Dàn and said:
“Alas!
The Shāng are entirely guilty.
I hope daily for counsel to establish achievements.
Counsel and words are often trustworthy,
but what should be done now?”
Zhōu Gōng said:
“The time has come.”
Then he raised an army and followed the old ways,
first employing the Three Unities;
first, unifying relatives to gain support,
second, employing the capable,
third, ensuring arrows are silent.
The Three Modesties are:
first, living near markets,
second, selling cheaply,
third, distributing wealth.
The Three Cares are:
first, borders not invading the interior,
second, roads not disturbing pastures,
third, suburbs not detaining people.
The Wáng said:
“Alas!
If one truly follows the Three,
and the Three are not thwarted,
their signs can be relied upon.
To love the Zhōu equally,
if love is subtle, there is no illness.
If illness causes one to take or not take,
if illness arrives, be prepared.
Crooked prayers are not virtuous,
not virtuous means no success.
Harm is not in the small,
ultimately it is truly great.
Regret afterwards is nonexistent.
Heaven's thoughts are not flattering.
Respond to the times with counsel,
not being diligent is dangerous!”
Zhōu Gōng said:
“These words are truly fitting.
Who will follow their own initiative?
If one acts but is not trustworthy, it leads to disaster.
If one goes but does not truly go, it leads to weakness.
May the officers and soldiers all be of one mind with Zhōu.”
On the first day of the fourth month, the King issued a warning.
He summoned Zhōu Gōng Dàn and said,
"Alas!
The plan has been leaked!
Now, when I awoke, the Shāng (dynasty) startled me.
I wished to grant them without measure,
I wished to attack them without merit.
To rule is insufficient.
Though warned, I have not prospered.
My sorrow is deep."
Zhōu Gōng said,
"The world fears Zhōu (dynasty),
and startled the King upon awakening.
May the King revere the mandate,
and follow the precedents of ancient kings.
Be able to enlighten the three virtues as principles,
pacify and harmonize distant peoples as merit.
Attack by means of prayer,
pardon the guilty,
cherish the multitudes,
then blessings will be granted.
Observe warnings regarding success and failure,
guard and protect them, do not lose them.
Do not give wings to a tiger,
lest it fly into the palace,
and choose people to devour.
Be neither arrogant nor miserly,
then you will have no enemies."
The King bowed and said,
"Indeed!
I have heard it said:
'Only when you consult with me,
then will our plans be good.
Not leaked, not exhausted,
that is only heaven's doing.'
I will, with you,
preserve the old ways.
All respectfully said:
'The later warnings are like those of old.'"
The way of Heaven honors the right;
the sun and moon move westward.
The way of Earth honors the left;
water flows in the middle.
The way of man honors the center;
ears and eyes serve the mind.
The mind has four assistants;
if they are not harmonious, it is called废 (fèi).
The Earth has five elements;
if they are not connected, it is called恶 (è).
Heaven has four seasons;
if they are not timely, it is called凶 (xiōng).
The way of Heaven is called 祥 (xiáng),
the way of Earth is called 义 (yì),
the way of man is called 礼 (lǐ).
To know 祥 (xiáng) is to live long,
to know 义 (yì) is to stand firm,
to know 礼 (lǐ) is to act.
When 礼 (lǐ), 义 (yì), and 祥 (xiáng) are in harmony, it is auspicious.
Auspicious 礼 (lǐ) returns to the left,
following Earth to benefit the foundation.
Martial 礼 (lǐ) returns to the right,
following Heaven to benefit the army.
The general occupies the central army,
following man to benefit the formation.
When a man has a center, he is called 参 (cān);
without a center, he is called 两 (liǎng).
When two contend, they are weak;
when three harmonize, they are strong.
A male is born and forms three,
a female is born and forms two.
Five complete a household,
a household is completed by the birth of people,
people by their measures.
The left and right hands each grasp five,
the left and right feet each tread five,
these are called the four limbs;
the head is called the extremity.
Five fives make twenty-five, called the primary卒 (zú).
One卒 (zú) in front is called 开 (kāi),
one卒 (zú) in back is called 敦 (dūn),
one卒 (zú) on the left and right is called 闾 (lǘ).
Four卒 (zú) form a guard called 伯 (bó),
three 伯 (bó) and one chief make a 佐 (zuǒ),
three 佐 (zuǒ) and one chief make a 右 (yòu),
three 右 (yòu) and one chief make a 正 (zhèng),
three 正 (zhèng) and one chief make a 卿 (qīng),
three 卿 (qīng) and one chief make a 辟 (bì).

a 卿 (qīng) must be benevolent,
a 正 (zhèng) must be wise,
a 右 (yòu) must be harmonious,
a 佐 (zuǒ) must be respectful,
a 伯 (bó) must be diligent,
a 卒 (zú) must be strong.

If a 卿 (qīng) is not benevolent, there is no way to gather the multitude.
If a 伯 (bó) is not diligent, there is no way to carry out orders.
If a 卒 (zú) is not strong, there is no way to receive instructions.
Uniformly strengthen the卒 (zú),
appear (brave) without turning back,
if they turn back, they will not be obedient.
Uniformly make the 伯 (bó) diligent,
work without slackening,
if they slacken, they will not be harmonious.
Uniformly make the 佐 (zuǒ) harmonious,
respectful without lingering,
if they linger, there will be no achievement.
Uniformly make the 右 (yòu) solemn,
reverent without shame,
if they are shameful, they will not prosper.
A 辟 (bì) must be cultivated,
sagely like a measure.
Primary loyalty honors humility,
kindness should benefit those below,
firmly gather steadfast virtue.
Speaking boldly without violating virtue is called 正 (zhèng).
When 正 (zhèng) reaches both gods and men, it is called 极 (jí).
One who can achieve 极 (jí) for generations is called 帝 (dì).
It is said, if we examine the ancients,
it is said, to illuminate the way of Heaven,
to expand the achievements of the 帝 (dì),
to measure the responsibilities of the people,
to regulate the use of virtue,
to unify all with abundance,
to equalize them with □ (unreadable character) prohibitions,
to perfect them with □ (unreadable character) harmony,
all will be peaceful among the people.
When the 卿 (qīng) arrive at the right time,
observing the various 辟 (bì),
respectfully considering the three affairs,
there will forever be blessings.
The three affairs:
First, to initiate virtue;
second, to harmonize chaos;
third, to complete order.
Virtue has seven guidelines,
chaos has five measures,
order has five preparations.
The five preparations:
First, to unify the path forward,
thereby measuring near and far.
Second, to make clear the essentials of ugly and friendly virtue,
thereby gathering your merits.
Third, to enlighten the 辟 (bì) and make them distant,
thereby solemnizing the people's teaching.
Fourth, to enlighten righteousness and encourage your multitude,
and teach them to obey.
Fifth, to grasp power and cultivated virtue,
not fearing the powerful and favored.
The five measures (for chaos):
First, to lead the unimpeded and resolve the obstructed.
Second, to eradicate without pardon and without doubt.
Third, to blunt sharpness without pardon and without danger.
Fourth, to rest the army without futility and without harm.
Fifth, to restore dignity, and those who abandon the group will be unmatched.
The seven guidelines (for virtue):
First, do not destroy cities with few defenders, do not take the road.
Second, do not carry loads on an open road.
Third, small states are not unlucky and are not attacked.
Fourth, righteousness is prosperity and tranquility without doubt.
Fifth, be harmonious and patient, bringing peace to the hundred clans.
Sixth, prohibit harm and seek to relieve the people.
Seventh, unify virtue to instruct the people,
and the people will be enlightened.
Be reverent, be reverent!
I seek this day and night without ceasing.
The King then went out to the territory of Shāng,
reaching Xiānyuán.
He summoned Zhào Gōng Shì and Bì Gōng Gāo.
The King said,
"Alas!
Be reverent!
There is no competition for man.
If man is truly loyal,
then affairs will be reverent.
Small men are difficult to protect.
When the ruler grants favor to the people,
the people will not fail to respond,
like the wind moving grass.
A bribe cannot achieve anything.
Continuous and unbroken,
how can creeping (vines) be stopped?
If even the finest tip is not picked,
it will become an axe handle."
The King then strengthened Yǐn Shì and the Eight Scholars,
only to firmly yield.
Virtue descended to become a model,
vibrating throughout the four quarters.
Their actions had good renown,
achieving harmony without opposition.
In addition, prayers were offered to shamans,
and gods and men were truly compliant.
Wáng Hè (王赫) valiantly raged,
the eight directions all arose.
High walls were like the ground,
the Shang (商) populace was as if transformed.
An appointment was made at Mù (牧).
Troops were deployed.
The Shang (商) were not to be exterminated.
Prayers were offered to the upper and lower (deities).
The King's meals were limitless.
The King did not break his word.
The populace forgave the established clan.
The eight scholars of the Yǐn (尹) clan,
the Grand Preceptor and Three Dukes,
all achieved merit.
No deity was un-honored.
The King was able to match Heaven,
uniting the four seas.
Thus, there was eternal peace.
Three hundred and fifty chariots of Zhōu (周)
were arrayed at Mùyě (牧野).
Dì Xīn (帝辛) followed.
Wǔ Wáng (武王) sent Shàngfǔ (尚父) and Bófū (伯夫) to issue the challenge.
The King then, with his tiger-fierce chariots, charged the Shang (商) army.
The Shang (商) army was greatly defeated.
Shāng Xīn (商辛) fled inward,
ascended the Lǐntái (廩臺) platform,
screened himself, and immolated himself in the fire.
Wǔ Wáng (武王) then, holding the great white banner, waved at the feudal lords.
The feudal lords all bowed,
and he then saluted them.
The common people of Shang (商) all waited in the suburbs.
All the guests together advanced and said:
"High Heaven sends down blessings."
They bowed twice and kowtowed.
Wǔ Wáng (武王) returned their bow.
First, he entered,
and went to the King's residence.
He then shot at it three times,
and only then dismounted his chariot.
He struck him with the Qīnglǚ (輕呂) sword,
and beheaded him with the Huángyuè (黃鉞) axe.
He severed the head and hung it from the great white banner.
He went to the residence of the two women, who had already hanged themselves.
The King again shot at them three times.
He then struck them with the Qīnglǚ (輕呂) sword,
and beheaded them with the Xuányuè (玄鉞) axe.
He hung their heads from the small white banner.
Then he emerged from his army.
The next day, he performed the rites for the altar of soil and the palace.
At the appointed time,
the hundred officers carried plain silk banners before the King.
Shú Zhèn (叔振) played music for the ceremonial bows.
He also arrayed the standard chariots.
Zhōu Gōng (周公) held the great axe.
Shào Gōng (召公) held the small axe,
flanking the King.
Tài Diān (泰顛) and Hóng Yāo (閎夭) both held the Qīnglǚ (輕呂) sword to guard the King.
The King entered,
took his place at the altar of soil,
to the left of the great army.

Shī Shàngfǔ (師尚父) led the sacrificial animal.

was bewildered by the clarity of the former Chéng Tāng (成湯).

Then he ordered Nángōng Bǎidá (南宮百達), Shǐ Yì (史佚) to move the nine cauldrons and three shamans.

In the thirteenth year,
the King was in Guǎn (管).
Guǎn Shú (管叔) made himself the overseer of Yīn (殷).
The lords of the eastern regions all received gifts from the King.
The King then journeyed to the eastern regions with them,
using the great rectification of the nine principles, eight dwellings, and six positions.
He was generous, modest, reverent,
stern day and night.
Manifest purity is not simplicity;
simplicity, if not clear,
clarity, if held privately,
private crookedness is not balanced;
balance, if loyal to desires,
cleverness thinks of ugly deception.
Manifest trustworthiness is not expansion;
expansion, if not exhausted by integrity,
integrity speaks of sincerity;
sincerity thinks of ugly slander.
Manifest yielding is not backing away;
backing away, if partisanship obstructs virtue,
virtue yields to respect;
respect thinks of worthy and hates contention.
Manifest position is not anger;
anger is not straightforward;
straightforwardness stands among the multitude;
straightforwardness thinks of ugly partiality.
Manifest governance is not idleness;
idleness is not distant regulation;
regulation governs progress;
progress thinks of ugly cruelty.
Manifest tranquility is not poverty;
poverty dwelling is not intention;
intention moves to action;
tranquility thinks of ugly restlessness.
Manifest purity is not doing;
doing, if impoverished, is not clean;
cleanliness purifies action;
action thinks of righteousness and hates greed.
Manifest cause is not haste;
haste is not unchaste;
chastity is firm in affairs;
firmness thinks of responsibility and hates extravagance.
When the nine principles are manifest,
the nine uglinesses naturally rectify themselves.
Rectification is called wisdom;
perversity is called brave unto death.

and the Huáshì will perish.
If one is fond of wealth, treasures, and exotic goods,
then wicked people will advance.
If wicked people advance,
then the worthy and good will be daily obscured and alienated,
and rewards and punishments will have no proper place,
but will be administered according to wealth.
The Xiàhòushì thus perished.
If one is severe with military power but does not [ ] it,
then one’s ministers will be intimidated.
If one’s ministers are intimidated and dare not be loyal,
and dare not be loyal,
then the people will not be close to their officials.
Punishments will begin with those close by,
and those far away will be disheartened.
The Yīnshāng thus perished.
If pleasure is monopolized by the sovereign,
then power will be monopolized by the ministers.
If power is monopolized by the ministers,
then punishment will be monopolized by the people.
The sovereign will be amused by pleasure,
the ministers will contend for power,
and the people will be exhausted by punishments.
The Yǒuyúshì thus perished.
Those who uphold orphans to issue exclusive commands,
their strategizing masters will surely fear their might and doubt their past actions.
Clutching virtue and demanding accountability will daily alienate them.
If positions are equal and there is contention,
the Pínglín thus perished.
If great ministers hold entrenched positions and clamor for executions, they are in danger.
In the past, the three ministers of Zhìshā,
when they attended court, were disrespectful.
The ruler was angered and detained them for a long time.
They clamored but were not punished further.
The clamoring ministers plotted rebellion,
and Zhìshā thus perished.
If internal and external factions are at odds,
and the lower ranks disturb their people,
and the people have nowhere to attach themselves,
the Sānmiáo thus perished.
If the small and weak are caught between the strong and great,
and their survival or demise will be determined by this,
then there is no heavenly mandate.
Those who do not know their destiny will die.
When the Xià was just rising,
the Hùshì was weak and disrespectful,
and its ruler died and its state perished.
If favored sons are both equally honored, it leads to ruin.
In the past, the Yìqúshì had two sons,
from different mothers, both equally honored.
When the ruler fell ill,
the great ministers divided into factions and contended,
and Yìqú thus perished.
Those whose great merits are not rewarded are in danger.
In the past, a minister of Píngzhōu,
whose merits were great but unrewarded,
while sycophantic ministers were daily rewarded and honored,
the meritorious minister grew angry and caused a rebellion,
and the ruler of Píngzhōu thus fled.
Those who summon distant people but do not treat them intimately are in danger.
In the past, the Yǒulínshì summoned the ruler of the Líróng and held court with him.
When he arrived, he was not treated with courtesy;
when he remained, he was not treated intimately.
The Líróng escaped and left.
The Yǒulínshì executed him,
and all under heaven rebelled against the Yǒulínshì.
In the past, the ruler of Qǔjí,
boasted of his wisdom and monopolized affairs,
exercising strong power but not demeaning his ministers.
The loyal and good all submitted silently.
The Yúzhōushì attacked him.
The ruler was isolated and had no agents,
and Qǔjí thus perished.
In the past, the Yǒucháoshì had a rebellious minister who was honored.
He was entrusted with the state,
and granted power.
He usurped the state and made all decisions.
After the ruler died, he was deprived of his power.
The minister grew angry and caused a rebellion,
and Yǒucháo thus perished.
If the axe is small and cannot overcome the handle, it leads to ruin.
In the past, the ruler of Kuài was frugal and thrifty,
diminishing titles and reducing emoluments.
His ministers were humble and yielded.
Superiors and subordinates had no oversight.
Later, when [the state] was small and weak,
prohibitions and punishments were not enforced.
The Zhòngshì attacked it,
and the ruler of Kuài thus perished.
Those who leave important positions vacant for a long time are in danger.
In the past, Gònggōng considered himself wise,
believing he had no need of ministers.
He left major offices vacant for a long time.
Subordinate officials became disorderly,
and the people had nowhere to attach themselves.
The Tángshì attacked him,
and Gònggōng thus perished.
Those who contend for power despite difficulties and are doubtful will die.
In the past, the Línshì and the Shànghéngshì contended for power.
The Línshì won two battles,
but the Shànghéngshì, feigning righteousness, failed to overcome them.
Both rulers died and their states perished.
Those whose knowledge and ability are equal but are not intimate,
and both are equally important in serving the ruler, are in danger.
In the past, the Nánshì had two ministers who were honored and favored.
Their power was equal and their influence rivalrous.
They continually advanced and contended for power.
Below, they contended for factions.
The ruler did not prohibit it,
and the Nánshì thus divided.
In the past, the Guǒshì liked to replace the old with the new.
The old became resentful and displeased.
The new and old were not in harmony.
Internally, they contended for factions,
and secretly lent power to external forces.
The Yǒuguǒshì thus perished.
If titles are heavy and emoluments are light,
and ratios [ ] are not achieved, it leads to ruin.
In the past, the Bìchéngshì
reduced emoluments and increased titles.
The ministers outwardly lacked [resources].
Comparing them, it caused popular discontent.
The Bìchéngshì thus perished.
Those who like to change old customs and alter established norms will perish.
The ruler of the Yángshì in the past
boasted of himself and liked to change.
Affairs had no fixed basis,
and offices had no fixed positions.
The people struggled below.
The Yángshì thus perished.
Those whose actions are apparent but are obstinate are in danger.
In the past, the ruler of Gǔpíng
was obstinate and without close kin.
His state was broken and he could not overcome it.
His actions were apparent in managing the state.
Internal and external forces supported each other.
Gǔpíng thus perished.
Those who do not cease military action will perish.
In the past, the Bǎnquánshì endlessly used military force,
constantly engaging in punitive wars.
He annexed and absorbed without forming close relations.
Culture had no place to be established.
Wise scholars were disheartened.
He relocated to Dúlù.
The feudal lords rebelled against him,
and Bǎnquán thus perished.
Those who are stubborn and have no close relations will perish.
In the past, the ruler of Xuánzōng
was stubborn and would not listen.
His officials did not follow his commands.
Those in charge of clan duties doubted whether to initiate major undertakings.
The ministers disintegrated.
The state achieved no accomplishments,
and Xuánzōng thus perished.
In the past, Xuándū favored ghost doctrines,
abandoned human affairs to serve heaven.
Strategizing ministers were not used.
Turtle shells and milfoil stalks were followed.
Divine shamans governed the state.
Wise scholars were outside,
and Xuándū thus perished.
Those in whom civil and military governance do not function will perish.
In the past, Xīxià was inherently benevolent and against warfare.
City walls were not repaired.
Warriors had no positions.
He was kind and fond of rewarding,
but his treasury was depleted and he had nothing to reward with.
The Tángshì attacked him.
The city walls could not be defended.
The warriors were not used,
and Xīxià thus perished.
Beautiful women can ruin a state.
In the past, Jìyáng was strong and powerful, conducting campaigns in all four directions.
The Zhòngqiū gifted him beautiful women.
The ruler of Jìyáng delighted in them.
He was confused and did not govern.
Great ministers contended for power.
Near and far did not listen to each other,
and the state divided into two.
Palaces can ruin a state.
In the past, the Yǒuluòshì had unceasing palace construction.
Ponds and parks were vast.
Labor and work progressed daily.
later and further on,
the people got no rest,
farmers missed their season,
and in famine they had no food.
Chéng Shāng (成商) attacked him,
and Yǒu Luò (有洛) perished.”
The Zhí Fāng Shì (職方氏) were in charge of the maps of All-under-Heaven,
distinguishing the people of its states and territories, cities and towns, the Four 夷 (Yí), Eight 蠻 (Mán), Seven 閩 (Mǐn), Nine 貉 (Hé), Five 戎 (Róng), and Six 狄 (Dí),
together with their resources, the number of their nine grains and six livestock.
They were thoroughly informed of their advantages and disadvantages.
Then they distinguished the states of the Nine Zhōu (九州),
so that they would share in common benefits.

its mountain range was called Huìjī (會稽);
its marshes and swamps were called Jùqū (具區);
its rivers were the Three Jiāng (三江);
its soaking waters were the Five Hú (五湖);
its advantages were gold, tin, bamboo, and arrows;
its people were two men to five women;
its livestock were suitable for chickens, dogs, birds, and beasts;
its grains were suitable for □.

its mountain range was called Héngshān (衡山);
its marshes and swamps were called Yúnmèng (雲夢);
its rivers were the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢);
its soaking waters were the Yǐng (潁) and Zhàn (湛);
its advantages were cinnabar, silver, ivory, and leather;
its people were one man to two women;
its livestock were suitable for birds and beasts;
its grains were suitable for rice.
