its mountain range was called Huàshān (華山);
its marshes and swamps were called Pǔtián (圃田);
its rivers were the Yíng (熒) and Luò (雒);
its soaking waters were the Bēizhà (陂溠);
its advantages were forests, lacquer, silk, and hemp;
its people were two men to three women;
its livestock were suitable for the six tamed animals;
its grains were suitable for the five kinds.
Directly east was called Qīngzhōu (青州);
its mountain range was called Yíshān (沂山);
its marshes and swamps were called Wàngzhū (望諸);
its rivers were the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗);
its soaking waters were the Yí (沂) and Shù (沭);
its advantages were rushes and fish;
its people were two men to three women;
its livestock were suitable for chickens and dogs;
its grains were suitable for rice and wheat.
East of the River (Hé) was called Yǎnzhōu (兗州);
its mountain range was called Dàishān (岱山);
its marshes and swamps were called Dàyě (大野);
its rivers were the Hé (河) and Jǐ (泲);
its soaking waters were the Lúwéi (盧維);
its advantages were rushes and fish;
its people were two men to three women;
its livestock were suitable for the six tamed animals;
its grains were suitable for the four kinds.
Directly west was called Yōngzhōu (雍州);
its mountain range was called Yuèshān (嶽山);
its marshes and swamps were called Xiánpú (弦蒲);
its rivers were the Jīng (涇) and Ruì (汭);
its soaking waters were the Wèi (渭) and Luò (洛);
its advantages were jade and stone;
its people were three men to two women;
its livestock were suitable for cattle and horses;
its grains were suitable for broomcorn millet and foxtail millet.
Northeast was called Yōuzhōu (幽州);
its mountain range was called Yīwúlǘ (醫無閭);
its marshes and swamps were called Wèiyǎng (貕養);
its rivers were the Hé (河) and Jǐ (泲);
its soaking waters were the Zī (菑) and Shí (時);
its advantages were fish and salt;
its people were one man to three women;
its livestock were suitable for the four tamed animals;
its grains were suitable for the three kinds.
Within the River (Hé) was called Jìzhōu (冀州);
its mountain range was called Huòshān (霍山);
its marshes and swamps were called Yángwéi (楊紆);
its river was the Zhāng (漳);
its soaking waters were the Fén (汾) and Lù (露);
its advantages were pine and cypress;
its people were five men to two women;
its livestock were suitable for cattle and sheep;
its grains were suitable for broomcorn millet and foxtail millet.
Directly north was called Bìngzhōu (并州);
its mountain range was called Héngshān (恒山);
its marshes and swamps were called Zhāoyúqí (昭餘祁);
its rivers were the Hūchí (虖池) and Ōuyí (嘔夷);
its soaking waters were the Láiyì (淶易);
its advantages were cloth and silk;
its people were two men to three women;
its livestock were suitable for the five tamed animals;
its grains were suitable for the five kinds.
Then they distinguished the states of the Nine Fú (九服):
A thousand *lǐ* square was called Wángqí (王圻), the royal domain;
beyond it, five hundred *lǐ* square was the Hóufú (侯服), domain of the marquises;
and beyond that, five hundred *lǐ* square was the Diànfú (甸服), domain of cultivation;
and beyond that, five hundred *lǐ* square was called Nánfú (男服), domain of the barons;
and beyond that, five hundred *lǐ* square was the Cǎifú (采服), domain of tribute;
and beyond that, five hundred *lǐ* square was the Wèifú (衛服), domain of defense;
and beyond that, five hundred *lǐ* square was called Mánfú (蠻服), domain of the Mán;
and beyond that, five hundred *lǐ* square was the Yífú (夷服), domain of the Yí;
and beyond that, five hundred *lǐ* square was the Zhènfú (鎮服), domain of pacification;
and beyond that, five hundred *lǐ* square was the Fānfú (藩服), domain of the fences.
As for all states:
the gōng (公), hóu (侯), bó (伯), zǐ (子), and nán (男) ranks were used to fully know All-under-Heaven.
As for all states and territories,
large and small supported each other.
The King established his herders (governors)
and regulated their duties, each according to their abilities.
He regulated their tributes, each according to their possessions.
When the King was about to undertake a巡狩 (xúnshòu) (inspection tour),
he would issue a warning to the four quarters, saying:
“Each of you, cultivate and bring order to your territories,
examine your official duties,
and dare not to be disrespectful or neglectful.
If a state has a major penalty,
or wherever the King's path of travel leads,
lead your subordinates and inspect and warn with orders.”
When the King held a grand ceremony in a state,
it was also like this.
King Lì lost the Way.
The Earl of Ruì presented his admonition,
which was composed by Ruì Liángfū.
The Earl of Ruì spoke thus:
“I, your humble minister Liángfū,
have carefully investigated the Way and reverently make this admonition.
The Son of Heaven is truly the father and mother of the people.
If he carries out his Way,
none, however distant, will fail to submit.
If he is without the Way,
his close ministers and concubines will deviate.
The people will turn to virtue;
if there is virtue, the people will support him;
if there is no virtue, the people will consider him an enemy.
These words have been truly effective
in the not-so-distant past:
Shāng Zhòu did not change the cruelty of Xià Jié,
and thus our Zhōu possessed the realm.
Alas!
You, the Son of Heaven,
succeed to the enterprise of Wén and Wǔ.
You, the young ministers in charge of government,
are the same as the ministers of the former kings.
In your muddled conduct, you fail to look back;
you lead the king to behave improperly.
You monopolize profit and exercise tyranny,
aiding disorder and advancing calamity.
The people will not be able to bear it.
Order and disorder truly depend on their actions.
This is something you, O King, and you, young ministers in charge of government, have heard.
The ancients sought much listening to use for caution and warning.
If one does not hear,
this is simply ignorance.
You hear and you know,
yet you do not change your ways;
this is indeed difficult.
A ruler eliminates harm for the people;
if he does not eliminate harm for the people,
but harms the people, then he is not a ruler,
but their enemy.
A ruler acts as an example;
if a ruler does not act as an example,
the people will not know the ruler,
but will resent him.
The people number in the hundreds of millions;
the ruler is but one.
The few cannot contend with the many;
the ruler is truly in peril!
Alas!
Domesticated animals are tamed by humans,
while wild birds flee when they see humans.
This is not due to the nature of birds and beasts;
in reality, the people are also like this.
Now, you young ministers in charge of government,
you serve the King only with greed and flattery,
not diligently cultivating virtue to prepare for difficulties.
The lower people resent each other,
their resources and strength exhausted,
their hands and feet unable to act.
They cannot bear to support the top.
Will there not be chaos?
As for me, your humble minister Liángfū,
I observe the lords of the land under Heaven:
their virtue is not far from yours,
none has a substitute for virtue.
At such a time, the King's troubles
will come from the people of the state.
Alas!
You, young ministers and friends in charge of government,
you should cleanse your hearts,
change your conduct,
and be able to regret past transgressions,
to preserve your positions.
If you are deaf to disaster and oblivious to calamity,
persisting in wrongdoing without repentance,
I do not know what the King’s destiny will be,
much less your own.
Calamity arises from what people overlook,
from what people take lightly.
If the mind is not attentive to it,
change lies hidden.
You young ministers in charge of government,
you do not consider great difficulties;
you live idly and seek temporary ease.
Appointments are achieved through bribery;
the wise and capable are silenced;
petty men wag their tongues.
They escape harm and seek profit,
and all get what they seek.
I can only say:
‘Alas!’
I have heard it said:
‘If you judge a person by their words,
they will embellish their words;
if you judge a person by their actions,
they will exhaust their actions.
Embellished words are useless;
exhausted actions bring accomplishment.’
You young ministers,
you embellish your words to serve the King,
and indeed you have many followers.
The King outwardly accepts them,
but in the end, they are not used.
You deceive each other to your faces,
until your downfall.
You yourselves say you have more than enough;
I say you are not enough.
Think carefully with virtue,
and prepare for your calamities.
If difficulties arrive and then you regret,
to what will your regret extend?
Do not say, ‘I acted’;
it will be your own disaster.”
The Duke Píng of Jìn sent Shūyù to Zhōu.
He met Prince Jìn and conversed with him.
He spoke five times and was stumped five times.
He retreated hesitantly,
his words unfulfilled.
Upon returning, he reported to the Duke, saying:
"Prince Jìn is but fifteen years of age,
yet your minister could not converse with him.
May Your Grace please return the land and tribute,
for if he does not return it,
when he comes to possess the world,
he will make it a cause for punishment."
Duke Píng was about to return it,
but Shī Kuàng objected, saying:
"Please allow your blind minister to go and speak with him.
If he can confound me,
then return and restore it."
Shī Kuàng met the Prince and praised him, saying:
"I have heard that the Prince's words
are loftier than Mount Tàishān.
Sleeping at night, I could not rest;
dwelling by day, I was uneasy.
Not minding the long journey,
I seek a single word."
The Prince replied:
"I heard that the Grand Music Master was coming.
I am greatly pleased and yet also afraid.
I am very young,
and seeing you, I am awestruck,
having completely forgotten my demeanor."
Shī Kuàng said:
"I heard that the Prince is a gentleman of antiquity,
most accomplished yet not arrogant.
From Jìn to Zhōu,
you traveled without knowing weariness."
The Prince replied:
"The gentlemen of antiquity
were most cautious in their actions.
Accumulating provisions and setting up barriers,
there were no limits to their roads.
The hundred surnames rejoiced in them
and followed them afar.
People from afar came with joy,
seeing the road as but a foot."
Shī Kuàng commended him,
and further praised him, saying:
"The gentlemen of antiquity,
their conduct is exemplary.
From Shùn downwards,
who possessed broad virtue?"
The Prince replied:
"One like Shùn is Heaven.
Shùn dwelt in his place
to benefit the world,
supporting and assisting people from afar,
all achieving their own benevolence.
This is called Heaven.
One like Yǔ
was a sage who toiled but did not reside
to benefit the world.
He liked to take but disliked to give,
yet he invariably measured its correctness.
This is called Sage.
One like King Wén
had a great path of benevolence,
and a small path of graciousness.
He possessed two-thirds of the world,
respected people without limits,
and served Shāng.
Though he had his multitudes, he lost his own person.
This is called Benevolence.
One like King Wǔ
righteously killed one man to benefit the world.
Those of different surnames and those of the same surname
each found their proper place. This is called Righteousness."
Shī Kuàng commended him,
and further praised him, saying:
"Clearly distinguish names and mandates,
differentiate wicked factions.
Kings, marquises, lords, and dukes,
how are they honored?
How are they supreme?"
The Prince replied:
"When a man is born, he is valued as a brave one,
and is called a zhòuzǐ.
When a zhòuzǐ becomes an adult
and can govern higher officials,
he is called a shì.
When a shì leads the multitude to work in due season,
he is called a bó.
When a bó can transfer goodness to the multitude
and be one with the hundred surnames,
he is called a gōng.
When a gōng can establish a name
and create things in harmony with the Way of Heaven,
he is called a hóu.
When a hóu can form a group, he is called a jūn.
When a jūn has broad virtue,
distributes responsibilities to the various marquises, and strengthens trust,
he says:
'I, the One Man.'
When his goodness reaches the Four Seas,
he is called the Tiānzǐ.
When it extends to the Four Wastes,
he is called the Tiānwáng.
When the Four Wastes arrive
and no one harbors resentment or criticism,
then he ascends to become a Dì."
Shī Kuàng was deeply impressed,
and further praised him, saying:
"Gentle, respectful, earnest, and keen,
steadfast in virtue without change,
hearing things [text missing]
learning from below to rise,
still ascending to become a minister to the Dì,
then participating with the Tiānzǐ,
who among the ancients was such?"
The Prince replied:
"Grand and revered was Yú Shùn,
bright and illustrious!
He established righteousness and regulated laws,
and all things flourished.
He equally distributed Heaven's wealth,
and all things were joyful and thriving.
If not Shùn, then who?"
Shī Kuàng stamped his foot, saying:
"Excellent!
Excellent!"
The Prince said:
"Grand Music Master, why do you raise your foot so quickly?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"The weather is cold, and my feet are stamping;
that is why it is frequent."
The Prince said:
"Please come in and sit."
Thereupon, he spread a mat and tuned a se.
Shī Kuàng sang "Wúshè," saying:
"The state is truly peaceful;
people from afar come to observe.
Righteousness is cultivated and regulated;
loving music, there is no excess."
Then he handed the se to the Prince.
The Prince sang "Jiào," saying:
"From the utmost South
to the utmost North,
crossing distant lands and traversing states,
one does not worry about the long road."
Shī Kuàng abruptly rose, saying:
"Your blind minister requests to depart."
The Prince bestowed upon him a carriage and four horses, saying:
"Grand Music Master, you are also skilled at driving them."
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Driving,
I have not learned."
The Prince said:
"Do you not recite that poem?
The poem says:
'The horse is strong,
the reins are soft.
The horse is not too strong,
the reins are not too soft.
Spirits high and bold,
taking and giving without doubt.'
Drive with this."
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Your blind minister has no sight
to discern for people.
I rely solely on my ears,
yet my ears also hear little and are easily stumped.
Prince,
will you become the宗 of the world?"
The Prince said:
"Grand Music Master,
why do you mock me?
From Tàihào down to Yáo, Shùn, and Yǔ,
there has never been a single clan that held the world twice.
If one is great at the right time but does not boast,
how can one obtain Heaven?
Moreover, I heard you know the length of people's lives;
tell me."
Shī Kuàng replied:
"Your voice is clear and thin,
your complexion is red and white.
A fiery complexion does not portend longevity."
The Prince said:
"Indeed, three years from now,
I shall ascend as a guest to the Emperor's abode.
You must be careful not to speak of this,
lest calamity befall you."
Shī Kuàng returned,
and less than three years passed,
when news of the Prince's death arrived.
What the jade wearer values is virtue.
Virtue lies in benefiting the people.
The people's state lies in obeying the superior.
All combined, it lies in adapting to the times.
Responding to affairs makes them easy to accomplish.
Achieving plans lies in thoroughness.
Having merit lies in abundant effort.
Grand prosperity lies in self-restraint.
Avoiding transgression lies in frequent correction.
Avoiding distress lies in foresight and caution.
Seeing misfortune lies in its unformed state.
Removing harm lies in being decisive.
Securing the people lies in acknowledging mistakes.
Employing troops lies in knowing the opportune moment.
Overcoming great calamities lies in uniting people's hearts.
Calamity and poison lie in trusting the doubtful.
Rebellious sons lie in listening to internal affairs.
Effective transformation lies in knowing harmony.
Bestowing generosity lies in an impartial mind.
Misfortune lies in not hearing one's faults.
Fortune lies in accepting counsel.
Foundation lies in loving the people.
Security lies in being close to the worthy.
Calamity and fortune lie in whom one is intimate with.
Benefit and harm lie in whom one is close to.
Survival and demise lie in whom one employs.
Separation and unity lie in issuing commands.
Respect lies in being cautious with authority.
Peace lies in being respectful of oneself.
Peril and demise lie in not knowing the opportune moment.
To see good and be lazy,
to have the moment arrive and hesitate,
to abandon the upright and dwell in wickedness –
these are things one cannot abide.
These are the methods of gain and loss,
which must not be left unexamined.
Tāng 將 (jiāng) to exile Jié (Jié) in the central wilderness.
